latin.59: Quinta & ultima ratio his verbis concepta est § XI. pag. 224. Ea interpretatio confirmatur vers. 13. sequenti, qui per particulam γάρ connectitur cum precedenti. Dubitare enim aliquis potuit, an omnes homines revera peccaverint; Id igitur Apostolus probat eo argumento, quod ubicunque mors est, ibi necesse est esse peccatum. Mors autem non extitit modo, sed & regnavit in omnes illos qui vixerunt iis temporibus, quae inter primum peccatum Adami & legem interfluxerunt: omnes illi ergo fuerunt peccato obnoxii. Respondeo inquit D. G. Abfit vero ut ejusmodi analysim accipiamus, quae ex divino Apostolo facit ineptum circulatorem. [§ XVIII.] Bona verba: ineptum circulatorem! Abfit a nobis tam grande crimen. Quomodo vero id probat? Nam, inquit, Apostolus versu 12. probat omnes esse addictos morti, quia peccaverunt, postea vers. 13. probat omnes peccasse, quia morti addicti sunt, & mors in omnes regnat. Hoc scilicet est esse ineptum circulatorem.
latin.60: Atqui non dixit illius rationis eruditissimus autor, Apostolum versu 12. probare, omnes esse addictos morti? Relege quaeso & considera rationem, quemadmodum ab ipso Garissolio recitata fuerat § XI. & a me exscripta. Num tale quid in ea animadvertis? aut ex ea bona consequentia deduci potest? Eccur vero Apostolus id probare instituisset, quod Scriptura, & omnium seculorum experientia, genusque adeo humanum universum perpetuo confitetur & clamat? Ecquis etiam credat, Apostolum probare voluisse clarius per obscurius? Clarius enim est omnes mori, quam omnes peccasse. Non igitur probat, sed ne viderentur omnes homines ob unicum unius hominis peccatum eis imputatum mori, affirmat per unum hominem ita mortem ingressam esse in genus humanum, ut non sola in omnes homines invaserit, sed ejus etiam causa, peccatum. Itaque mori omnes non proxime ob unum illud actuale unius hominis peccatum, sed ob suum quemque sibi insitum, ab illo derivatum. Fingit ergo D. G. probationem circularem ubi nulla est.
latin.61: quanquam si esset, non tam circulus a Philosophis damnatus, quam regressus ab iisdem laudatus dici deberet: constaret enim ex duabus demonstrationibus, altera τὸ ὅτι, altera τὸ διότι, illa pariente distinctam effectus, hac confusam causae notitiam. Eandem autem circulationem cum ipse sibi objecisset D. G. expedire sese ex ea non potuit. Posteriorem enim tantum rationem attigit, priorem, ex qua pendebat circulus, alto involvit silentio. Peto igitur ex ejus mente, num Apostolus probet vs. 12. omnes esse morti addictos, quia peccatum Adae ipsis imputatur? Si ais, manet circularis argumentatio: statim enim vs. 13. & 14. probabit omnibus peccatum Adae imputari, quia omnes sunt morti addicti. Si negas, tollis quidem circulum; sed neque id negavit D. G. neque ut se ex eo circulo educeret, quicquam ejusmodi tentavit: fecit ergo id, cujus nos falso accusabat, ex Apostolo divino ineptum, ut loquitur, circulatorem.
latin.62: Sed tamen inde hoc argumentum elicit. Quibus irrogatur poena mortis propter peccatum, iis peccatum imputatur. Atqui infantibus irrogata est ante legem poena mortis propter peccatum Adae. Ergo iis peccatum Adae imputatum est. Resp. Peccatum Adae duobus modis accipi: 1. pro eo peccato, quod ab eo in posteros propagatum & secundum hominum numerum multiplicatum, caro & vetus Adam appellatur. 2. pro causa peccati illius propagati, nempe actuali Adae inobedientia. Si priore modo accipitur, concedo totum argumentum. Fateor enim peccatum illud, quia intra nos est, nobis omnibus, etiam infantibus, merito imputari. Si posteriore modo, distinguo praepositionem propter: nam vel causam proximam seu immediatam, vel remotam tantum seu mediatam significat. Si prius, nego minorem propositionem: irrogata est infantibus poena mortis proxime ob inhaerens vitium, remote ob Adami actuale peccatum. Si posterius, inde sequitur duntaxat peccati illius actualis imputatio mediata, quam ultro concedo. Hoc me docuit Calvinus, quia, inquit, ejus peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus ascribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur. Et Bullingerus, non noceret nobis Adae lapsus, nisi talis ex eo perversitas seu corruptio nobis innata fuisset, quae Dei judicium promeretur.
latin.63: Sic vindicata est versio Gallica, qua utuntur Ecclesiae nostrae. Quod autem subjungit D. G. Sic acriter disputatum fuisse, &c, sed ab eo tempore deferbuisse impetum, in posterioribus scriptis mutata esse velificationem &c, Fallitur vehementer. Eadem enim perpetuo Placei sententia fuit, & melius verti voces ἐφ᾽ ᾧ eo quod, quam in quo. Et tamen ne hanc quidem versionem obesse sententiae suae, ob eas rationes, quas thesibus suis aliquot annis, priusquam Manuscriptum illud prius fieret, editis, inseruerat. Non viderat illud manuscriptum, cum suum istud fecit quod D. G. posterius appellat, nec cur mutaret, ut loquitur vir Doctus, velificationem causa ulla erat. Nemo enim ei tum quicquam objecerat, quo recepta, quam sequitur, vocularum ἐφ᾽ ᾧ versio impugnaretur. De nostra confessione, quam praeter rationem triumphet hoc loco D. G. patet ex dictis pag. hujus lib. 73. Quae tamen si ulla fuisset, Placeo obesse non posset, quo inscio nec consentiente facta fuisset. Sed de illa versione jam fortasse plus satis.
latin.64: Redeo ad argumentum supra pag. 70. ita propositum, ut ejus tres lineae a Typographo repetitae fuerint, nec a Correctore, adeo aliis distractus negotiis tunc festinabat, deletae. Id sic habet. Qui, cum nondum essent in rerum natura, dicuntur in alio peccasse, censentur proculdubio eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod evidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cum nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo peccasse. Ergo censentur eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi commisisse, quod ad imputationem peccati Adae manifeste pertinet. Primo nego id evidenter ad imputationem pertinere quam antecedentem seu immediatam voco. Cur enim non pertineat potius ad propagationem peccati inhaerentis, quod reatus & imputatio sequitur? Deinde nego majorem. An enim qui dicuntur in alio fuisse, vel mortui fuisse, censentur eo existente vel moriente & ipsi extitisse, & mortui fuisse? Morimur certe in Adamo, sed sua quisque morte; sicut resurgimus in Christo sua quisque resurrectione. Sic peccamus in Adamo, sed suo quisque peccato. Notatur tantum peccati & mortis primus autor & fons, unde ad nos omnes dimanarunt. Denique nego minorem. Non enim dixit Apostolus, omnes homines, cum nondum essent, in Adamo peccasse. Jam ostendi, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ non significare hoc loco in quo. Dixit quidem per unum hominem peccatum ita in mundum intrasse, ut omnes homines peccaverint, sed non dixit, peccasse in uno illo homine: Multo vero minus dixit tunc peccasse cum nondum essent in rerum natura. Hoc enim mihi videtur manifestam contradictionem implicare. Quis enim contradictionem implicari non videat, si quis dicat, prius esse accidens quam subjectum, prius homines fuisse peccatores quam homines, mortuos quam viventes, imo prius peccasse quam fuisse?

pass_a.59: The fifth and last reason is framed in these words at § XI, p. 224. That reading of ἐφ᾽ ᾧ is confirmed by the next verse, Romans 5:13, which is joined to what precedes by the particle γάρ. Someone might doubt whether all men truly sinned; so the Apostle proves it by this: wherever death is, there sin must be. Death not only appeared but reigned over all who lived in the times between Adam's first sin and the law; therefore all those were liable to sin. Doctor Garissoles answers: far be it that we accept such an analysis, which makes the divine Apostle an inept circular arguer (§ XVIII). Placeus: fine words — 'inept circular arguer'! Far be so great a crime from us. How does Garissoles prove the charge? He says Paul in verse 12 proves all are doomed to death because they sinned, then in verse 13 proves all sinned because they are doomed and death reigns over all — and that, he says, is being an inept circular arguer.
pass_a.60: Placeus rejects Garissoles's circular reading of the fifth reason. The learned author of that reason never claimed that Romans 5:12 is a proof that everyone is doomed to death. Read again the reason as Garissoles recited it in § XI and as Placeus transcribed it: nothing there yields that consequence cleanly. Paul would not labor to demonstrate what Scripture, every age's experience, and the entire human race already confess out loud. Nor would he prove what is clearer (that all die) by what is darker (that all have sinned). So verse 12 is not a proof of death. Its point is preventive: to keep readers from thinking people die for one man's single sin charged to them by imputation, Paul states that through one man death entered the race in such a way that sin — death's cause — entered with it. Death therefore falls on each immediately for his own implanted sin drawn from Adam, not immediately for Adam's one actual act. Garissoles fabricates a circular demonstration where the text has none.
pass_a.61: Even if there were a circle, it would better be called not the circle philosophers condemn but the regress they praise: it would consist of two demonstrations, one τὸ ὅτι (that the effect is), one τὸ διότι (why), the former yielding a distinct grasp of the effect, the latter a confused grasp of the cause. When Doctor Garissoles had objected this same circularity to himself, he could not get clear of it. He touched only the later reason and wrapped the prior one — on which the circle hung — in deep silence. Placeus asks him: does Paul in verse 12 prove all are doomed to death because Adam's sin is imputed to them? If yes, the circular argument remains: at once verses 13 and 14 will prove Adam's sin is imputed to all because all are doomed. If no, you remove the circle; but Garissoles neither denied that nor tried anything of the sort to escape the circle. So he did the very thing of which he falsely accused Placeus's side: he made the divine Apostle, as he puts it, an inept circular arguer.
pass_a.62: Yet from there Garissoles draws this argument: to those on whom the penalty of death is laid for sin, sin is imputed. But before the law the penalty of death for Adam's sin was laid on infants. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them. Placeus answers: Adam's sin is taken in two ways. (1) As the sin propagated from him into posterity and multiplied by the number of men — called flesh and the old Adam. (2) As the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If the first way, he grants the whole argument: that sin, because it is inside us, is rightly imputed to us all, even infants. If the second way, he distinguishes the preposition 'on account of' (propter): it can mean the near or immediate cause, or only the remote or mediate one. If the near sense, he denies the minor: infants' death-penalty is laid immediately for the inherent vice, remotely for Adam's actual sin. If the remote sense, only mediate imputation of that actual sin follows — which he freely grants. Calvin taught him this: because Adam's sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him; by 'our sin' Calvin means what is inborn and what we are born with. Bullinger: Adam's fall would not hurt us unless such perversity or corruption were inborn in us from it as would deserve God's judgment.
pass_a.63: So the French version used by our churches is vindicated. As for Garissoles's add-on — that the matter was fiercely disputed, but afterward the heat cooled and later writings changed tack, and so on — he is badly wrong. Placeus's view was the same throughout, and ἐφ᾽ ᾧ is better rendered 'because' (eo quod) than 'in whom' (in quo). Even so, that version does not hurt his position, for the reasons he had already put in theses published some years before that earlier manuscript existed. He had not seen that manuscript when he made the piece Garissoles calls later, and there was no reason to change tack, as the learned man puts it. No one had then objected anything by which the received rendering of the little words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ that he follows could be attacked. As for our confession, which Garissoles unreasonably triumphs over here, see what was said at p. 73 of this book. Even if there had been any such confession, it could not hurt Placeus, since it would have been made without his knowledge or consent. But perhaps enough already about that version.
pass_a.64: Placeus goes back to the syllogism printed earlier at page 70. The printer had duplicated three lines; the corrector, busy and rushing, left the duplicates undeleted. The argument claims: if people not yet existing are said to have sinned in someone else, then while that someone sins they themselves are counted as sinning too — and that clearly means imputation; but everyone is said to have sinned in Adam before existing; so while Adam sinned they too are counted as sinning — which clearly means imputation of Adam's sin. Placeus's first denial: that link does not clearly mean antecedent or immediate imputation; it fits better the spread of inherent sin, after which guilt and imputation come. Second denial — the major: being-said-to-have-been or died in another does not mean you yourself existed or died while he did. We die in Adam each by our own death, and rise in Christ each by our own rising; likewise we sin in Adam each by our own sin. Adam is marked only as first author and spring of sin and death flowing to us. Third denial — the minor: Paul never said all people sinned in Adam while they did not yet exist. ἐφ᾽ ᾧ here is not 'in whom.' Paul said sin entered through one man so that all sinned, not that they sinned inside that one man, and still less that they sinned then before they existed. That would put accident before subject: sinners before they were men, dead before alive, sinning before being.

59: The fifth and last reason is framed in these words (§ XI, p. 224): "That interpretation is confirmed by the following verse 13, which is joined to the preceding by the particle γάρ. For someone might doubt whether all men have truly sinned; the Apostle therefore proves it by this argument, that wherever death is, there sin must necessarily be. But death not only existed, but also reigned over all those who lived in the times that flowed between Adam's first sin and the law: all those, therefore, were liable to sin." "I answer," says Doctor Garissoles, "far be it that we should accept such an analysis, which makes of the divine Apostle an inept circular arguer" (§ XVIII). Fine words: an inept circular arguer! Far be so great a crime from us. But how does he prove it? "For," he says, "the Apostle in verse 12 proves that all are sentenced to death because they have sinned; afterward in verse 13 he proves that all have sinned because they are sentenced to death, and death reigns over all. This, of course, is to be an inept circular arguer."
60: And yet the most learned author of that reason did not say that the Apostle in verse 12 is proving that all are sentenced to death. Reread, I ask, and consider the reason as it had been recited by Garissoles himself at § XI and copied out by me. Do you notice anything of the kind in it? Or can a sound consequence be drawn from it? Why indeed would the Apostle have set about proving what Scripture, and the experience of every age, and the whole human race besides, forever confess and cry aloud? Who also would believe that the Apostle meant to prove the clearer by the obscurer? For that all die is clearer than that all have sinned. He does not, therefore, prove; but lest all men should seem to die on account of one man's one sin imputed to them, he affirms that through one man death so entered the human race that not death alone invaded all men, but also its cause — sin. And so all die not immediately on account of that one actual sin of one man, but on account of each man's own implanted in him, derived from that one. Doctor Garissoles therefore invents a circular proof where there is none.
61: And yet if there were one, it ought to be called not so much a circle condemned by the philosophers as a regress praised by the same: for it would consist of two demonstrations, one τὸ ὅτι, the other τὸ διότι — the former producing a distinct knowledge of the effect, the latter a confused knowledge of the cause. But when Doctor Garissoles had objected this same circularity to himself, he could not extricate himself from it. For he touched only the later reason; the prior one, on which the circle hung, he wrapped in deep silence. I ask, therefore, from his mind: does the Apostle in verse 12 prove that all are sentenced to death because Adam's sin is imputed to them? If you say yes, the circular argumentation remains: for at once in verses 13 and 14 he will prove that Adam's sin is imputed to all, because all are sentenced to death. If you deny it, you do indeed remove the circle; but neither did Doctor Garissoles deny that, nor did he attempt anything of the kind in order to lead himself out of that circle: he therefore did the very thing of which he falsely accused us — he made of the divine Apostle, as he speaks, an inept circular arguer.
62: Yet from there he draws out this argument: "To those on whom the penalty of death is inflicted on account of sin, sin is imputed. But before the law the penalty of death on account of Adam's sin was inflicted on infants. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them." I answer: Adam's sin is taken in two ways: (1) for that sin which, propagated from him into posterity and multiplied according to the number of men, is called flesh and the old Adam; (2) for the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If it is taken in the former way, I grant the whole argument. For I confess that that sin, because it is within us, is rightly imputed to us all, even to infants. If in the latter way, I distinguish the preposition "on account of": for it signifies either the near or immediate cause, or only the remote or mediate. If the former, I deny the minor proposition: the penalty of death was inflicted on infants immediately on account of the inherent vice, remotely on account of Adam's actual sin. If the latter, there follows only a mediate imputation of that actual sin, which I freely grant. Calvin taught me this, because, he says, Adam's sin is the cause of our sin, and Paul ascribes our ruin to him (Romans 5). "I call our sin," he says, "that which is inborn in us, and with which we are born." And Bullinger: "Adam's fall would not hurt us unless such perversity or corruption had been inborn in us from it as would deserve God's judgment" (Decades).
63: Thus the French version used by our churches is vindicated. But as for what Doctor Garissoles subjoins — that it had been fiercely disputed, and so on, but that from that time the heat cooled, that in later writings the tack was changed, and so on (§ XIX, p. 239) — he is vehemently mistaken. For Placeus's judgment was the same throughout, and the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ are better rendered "because" than "in whom." And yet not even this version harms his position, for those reasons which he had inserted in his theses published some years before that earlier manuscript was made. He had not seen that manuscript when he made that piece of his which Doctor Garissoles calls later, nor was there any cause why he should change tack, as the learned man speaks. For no one had then objected anything to him by which the received version of the little words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, which he follows, could be attacked. As for our confession, over which Doctor Garissoles triumphs beyond reason in this place, it is plain from what was said at page 73 of this book. And yet if there had been any, it could not hurt Placeus, since it would have been made without his knowledge or consent. But of that version perhaps already more than enough.
64: I return to the argument set out above at page 70 — so proposed that three of its lines were repeated by the typographer and not deleted by the corrector, so hurried was he then, distracted by other business. It runs thus: "Those who, when they were not yet in the nature of things, are said to have sinned in another are doubtless counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves also, which plainly pertains to imputation. But all men, when they were not yet, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves, which plainly pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin." First I deny that this plainly pertains to the imputation which I call antecedent or immediate. For why should it not rather pertain to the propagation of inherent sin, which guilt and imputation follow? Next I deny the major. For are those who are said to have been in another, or to have died, counted, while he existed or died, to have existed themselves and to have died? We certainly die in Adam, but each by his own death; just as we rise in Christ, each by his own resurrection. So we sin in Adam, but each by his own sin. Only the first author and fountain of sin and death is marked, from which they flowed out to us all. Finally I deny the minor. For the Apostle did not say that all men, when they were not yet, sinned in Adam. I have already shown that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ does not mean "in whom" in this place. He did say that through one man sin so entered into the world that all men sinned, but he did not say that they sinned in that one man: and much less did he say that they then sinned when they were not yet in the nature of things. For this seems to me to imply a plain contradiction. For who would not see a contradiction implied if someone should say that the accident was before the subject, that men were sinners before they were men, dead before living — indeed, that they sinned before they existed?
